instructions: 1. See who can stay the quietest for the longest amount of time. 2. Use a timer to set a goal (e.g., 1 minute). 3. The "winner" gets to choose the next game. 4. This is a great transition activity between high-energy play and quiet time. 5. Discuss why being quiet helps us listen and focus.

title: rocket trails
what you'll need: Paper, markers, long strips of paper
instructions: 1. Draw a rocket at the top of a page. 2. Glue long, colorful strips of paper (fire) to the bottom of the rocket. 3. Hold the rocket and run; the "trails" will flutter behind it. 4. Discuss how rockets need fire (thrust) to go into space. 5. Use the rocket for imaginative play.

title: ball pass
instructions: 1. Two children stand back-to-back. 2. They must work together to pass a ball from one to the other without turning around. 3. Try passing the ball over the head and then through the legs. 4. See how many times they can pass it without dropping it. 5. This builds trust and communication.

title: paper football game
description: this is for children to play with, I am not expecting them to be able to make it themselves.
instructions: 1. Fold a paper "football" (triangle). 2. Use your fingers to flick the football across a table toward a "goal" (made of lolly sticks). 3. Keep track of your points. 4. Discuss the rules of football. 5. Practice your "flicking" technique to get more power.

title: paper dolls for shelves or swings
instructions: 1. Draw paper dolls with long, flexible legs. 2. Place them on the edge of a shelf so their legs "dangle." 3. Build a "swing" out of string and a lolly stick. 4. Act out stories with the dolls in their new environment. 5. Discuss where the dolls might be going today.

title: spring snakes
instructions: 1. Cut a long strip of paper. 2. Draw snake patterns all over it. 3. Fold the paper into a tight accordion spring. 4. When you let go, the snake "jumps" or springs up. 5. Discuss how some snakes can move very quickly.

title: peg sloths
instructions: 1. Draw a sloth body (without legs) on brown cardstock. 2. Cut it out. 3. Clip wooden pegs to the arms and legs so the sloth can "hang" from a string or branch. 4. Move the sloth slowly along the line. 5. Discuss why sloths are so slow.

title: mini well
what you'll need: Cardboard box, string, lolly sticks, paper cup
instructions: 1. Build a "well" out of a cardboard box. 2. Use a skewer as the "axle" and wind string around it. 3. Attach a paper cup to the end of the string. 4. Turn the handle to "lower" and "raise" the bucket. 5. Discuss how people used wells to get water before we had taps.

title: wobble surfer
instructions: 1. Cut a surfer shape out of cardboard. 2. Tape a penny to the bottom of the "surfboard." 3. Place the surfer on a curved surface (like a bowl). 4. Give it a nudge and watch it "wobble" and surf without falling. 5. Discuss how the weight at the bottom provides stability.

title: balloon squahers
instructions: 1. Use a funnel to fill a balloon with flour. 2. Tie the end shut. 3. Squeeze the balloon; it will hold the shape of your hand. 4. This is a great "stress ball" for sensory input. 5. Observe how the balloon changes shape when you squash it.

title: fishing for ice cubes
description: WARNING: DO NOT TOUCH THE ICE AS IT IS REACTING WITH THE SALT, IT WILL BURN YOU. DO NOT LEAVE CHILD ALONE WITH SALT AND ICE.
instructions: 1. Place a piece of string over an ice cube. 2. Sprinkle salt over the string and ice. 3. Wait 30 seconds, then lift the string. 4. The ice will have "melted and refrozen" around the string, allowing you to lift the cube. 5. **WARNING**: Do not touch the salt/ice mixture with bare skin.

title: spinner
instructions: 1. Decorate a cardboard circle on both sides. 2. Poke two holes near the center and thread a string through. 3. Twirl the string and then pull it tight to make the disk spin and "hum." 4. Observe how the colors blend together. 5. This is a classic "spinner" toy.

title: mini golf
instructions: 1. Place paper cups on their side as "holes." 2. Use a lolly stick to "putt" a small ball into the cups. 3. Create a course with different obstacles. 4. Keep track of your "strokes." 5. Discuss the rules of golf.

title: Play dough/clay hedgehogs with sticks for spines
instructions: 1. Roll a ball of play dough into an oval shape for a hedgehog body. 2. Go outside and find small, thin twigs. 3. Poke the sticks into the back of the dough to create "spines." 4. Add small beads for eyes. 5. Discuss how hedgehogs use their spines for protection.

title: flipsticks
instructions: 1. Paint one side of a lolly stick one color and the other side a different color. 2. Toss the sticks and see how many land "color-side up." 3. Create a point system for the results. 4. This is a game of chance and counting. 5. Discuss the probability of certain colors appearing.

title: sussex nature reserve checklist
instructions: 1. Go to a nature reserve or park. 2. Use a checklist to find specific birds, plants, or insects. 3. Mark each item off as you find it. 4. Draw a picture of the most interesting thing you saw. 5. Discuss why it is important to protect nature reserves.

title: tree painting
what you'll need: Broccoli or sponges, green and brown paint, paper
instructions: 1. Paint a brown "trunk" on paper. 2. Dip a piece of broccoli or a sponge into green paint. 3. "Stamp" the leaves onto the branches. 4. Observe the realistic "leaf" texture created by the broccoli. 5. Add "apples" (red dots) with your finger.

title: bouncy balls
instructions: 1. Mix warm water and borax. 2. In a separate bowl, mix glue, cornstarch, and food coloring. 3. Combine the two mixtures and knead until firm. 4. Roll into a ball. 5. Test how high your "super bouncy ball" can jump.

title: what can i control poster?
instructions: 1. Draw a large circle. 2. Inside the circle, write things you *can* control (e.g., your words, your effort). 3. Outside the circle, write things you *cannot* control (e.g., the weather, others' actions). 4. Use this as a guide when you feel overwhelmed. 5. Discuss how focusing on what we can control makes us feel better.

title: dino footprints
instructions: 1. Dip the feet of toy dinosaurs into paint. 2. "Walk" the dinosaurs across a piece of paper. 3. Compare the different footprints (3 toes vs. 4 toes). 4. Try to match the dinosaur to its track. 5. Discuss how footprints are a type of "trace fossil."

title: thaumatrope
description: A thaumatrope is an optical toy that was popular in the 19th century. A disk with a picture on each side is attached to two pieces of string. When the strings are twirled quickly between the fingers the two pictures appear to blend into one due to the persistence of vision.
instructions: 1. Draw a bird on one side of a cardboard circle and a cage on the other. 2. Attach strings to the sides. 3. Twirl the disk rapidly. 4. The bird will appear to be *inside* the cage because of "persistence of vision." 5. Try other combinations, like a fish and a bowl.

title: paper rainbow
what you'll need: Strips of colored paper, glue, cotton balls
instructions: 1. Cut strips of paper in the colors of the rainbow. 2. Glue the ends of the strips to create an "arc." 3. Glue cotton ball "clouds" to each end of the rainbow. 4. Discuss the order of the colors (ROYGBIV). 5. Hang the rainbow in a window.

title: pom pom launcher
instructions: 1. Cut the bottom off a paper cup. 2. Tie a knot in an uninflated balloon and cut off the top. 3. Stretch the balloon over the bottom of the cup. 4. Place a pom-pom inside. 5. Pull the knot and release to launch the pom-pom!

title: balancetree
instructions: 1. Cut a vertical slit in a cardboard tube. 2. Take turns sliding lolly sticks into the slit. 3. The goal is to keep the "tree" balanced as you add more branches. 4. If the tree tips over, the game ends. 5. Discuss how weight distribution affects stability.

title: balloonkicking
instructions: 1. Try to keep a balloon in the air using *only* your feet. 2. Count how many "kicks" you can do before it hits the floor. 3. This builds leg-eye coordination. 4. Try playing with a partner. 5. Discuss why the balloon falls slowly compared to a real ball.

title: bearrescue
instructions: 1. "Trap" toy bears to a tray using masking tape. 2. The child must carefully peel the tape to "rescue" the bears. 3. Discuss the importance of being kind and helping others. 4. Once rescued, give the bear a "check-up." 5. This is a great empathy-building activity.

title: bouncingsnake
instructions: 1. Fold a paper snake into an accordion. 2. Tape one end to a surface and pull the other. 3. When you release it, the snake "bounces" back. 4. Discuss how the folds act like a spring. 5. See who can make the "bounciest" snake.

title: braidingboard
instructions: 1. Glue several clothespins to a piece of cardboard. 2. Practice "braiding" long pieces of yarn around the pins. 3. This builds the finger strength and sequencing skills needed for real braiding. 4. Use different colors of yarn to see the pattern clearly. 5. Discuss how we use braiding in hair and textiles.

title: brushyourteeth
what you'll need: Cardboard, white paint, dry-erase marker, toothbrush
instructions: 1. Draw a large set of "teeth" on cardboard and laminate or cover with tape. 2. Use a dry-erase marker to draw "germs" or food on the teeth. 3. Provide the child with a toothbrush and a little water. 4. Have them brush the cardboard teeth until all the marker spots are gone. 5. Discuss why brushing our own teeth is important for health.

title: buttoncaterpillar
instructions: 1. Cut out a small paper circle for a caterpillar head. 2. Thread a variety of colorful buttons onto a pipe cleaner. 3. Attach the head to the front of the pipe cleaner. 4. Bend the end of the pipe cleaner to keep the buttons from falling off. 5. Count the buttons to see how long the caterpillar has grown.

title: buttoncolours
instructions: 1. Provide a large bowl of mixed buttons in various colors and sizes. 2. Set out several cups that match the button colors. 3. Have the child sort the buttons into the correct cups. 4. To increase difficulty, ask them to sort by the number of holes (2 holes vs 4 holes). 5. Discuss the different shades and textures of the buttons.

title: buttondraw
instructions: 1. Draw a simple outline of a tree, flower, or balloon strings on paper. 2. Provide a variety of buttons to act as "leaves," "petals," or "balloons." 3. Apply small dots of glue to the paper. 4. Carefully place the buttons onto the glue. 5. Let the artwork dry completely before displaying.

title: buttonpaperchain
instructions: 1. Cut strips of paper and glue them into a standard paper chain. 2. Before closing each loop, slide a large-holed button onto the strip. 3. Alternatively, glue buttons onto the finished links in a specific pattern. 4. Use the chain to decorate a room or measure the length of a table. 5. Observe how the buttons add weight and texture to the paper.

title: buttonthreading
instructions: 1. Provide a long string with a large knot at one end. 2. Have the child thread buttons onto the string one by one. 3. Encourage them to create a pattern (e.g., small-large-small). 4. Tie the ends together to create a necklace or a "button snake." 5. This is an excellent activity for developing the pincer grip.

title: carcolourtrace
what you'll need: Toy cars, colored markers, large paper
instructions: 1. Draw winding roads on a large sheet of paper using different colored markers. 2. Have the child choose a car that matches the color of a specific road. 3. "Drive" the car along the line, staying as close to the center as possible. 4. Cross the roads to add a challenge. 5. Discuss the different "routes" the cars are taking.

title: carparknumbermatch
instructions: 1. Draw a "car park" on a sheet of cardboard with numbered parking bays. 2. Label toy cars with matching numbers using small stickers. 3. Have the child "park" each car in its corresponding numbered bay. 4. Ask them to count the cars as they park them. 5. Practice "reverse parking" for a motor skill challenge.

title: caterpillarcounting
instructions: 1. Place a card with a number (1-10) next to a caterpillar head. 2. Have the child roll that number of play dough balls. 3. Line the balls up behind the head to create the body. 4. Count the segments out loud. 5. Swap the number and adjust the body length accordingly.

title: catogorising
instructions: 1. Mix up a variety of items (e.g., toy animals, utensils, blocks). 2. Ask the child to sort them into groups (e.g., "things that are blue" vs "things that are red"). 3. Discuss why each item belongs in its group. 4. Re-sort the same items by a different rule, like size or material. 5. This builds the foundational logic for scientific classification.

title: catogorising2
instructions: 1. Provide a bowl of dried pasta (bowties, penne, spirals). 2. Have the child sort the pasta by shape into separate bins. 3. Count how many are in each bin. 4. Use the sorted pasta to create a repeating pattern on the table. 5. Discuss the different textures and names of the shapes.

title: catogorising3
instructions: 1. Go on a nature walk and collect "loose parts." 2. Sort the items by type (all leaves in one pile, all stones in another). 3. Re-sort the leaves by color or the stones by weight. 4. Discuss where each item came from. 5. Use the sorted items to build a nature mandala.

title: catogorising4
what you'll need: Plastic animals, sorting mats (Land, Sea, Air)
instructions: 1. Set out three mats representing different habitats. 2. Provide a bin of mixed plastic animals. 3. Have the child place each animal on the mat where it lives. 4. Discuss why a whale can't live on land or a bird in the deep sea. 5. Name the animals as they are placed.

title: catogorising5
instructions: 1. Dump a pile of clean laundry on the floor. 2. Have the child sort the items by person or by type (e.g., all the socks together). 3. Practice matching pairs of socks. 4. Count how many items belong to each family member. 5. This integrates math skills into real-world helpfulness.

title: catogorising6
instructions: 1. Provide a mix of clean plastic, paper, and metal items. 2. Have the child sort the items into the correct recycling bins. 3. Discuss what happens to the items after they are recycled. 4. Identify the "recycling symbol" on different packages. 5. Talk about why we try to reduce waste.

title: chainpattern
instructions: 1. Create a set of "pattern cards" showing color sequences (e.g., Red-Blue-Red). 2. Provide the child with paper strips in matching colors. 3. Have the child build a paper chain that follows the card exactly. 4. Connect the chains together to make a long "pattern snake." 5. Discuss what color comes next in the sequence.

title: citystack
what you'll need: Wooden blocks or boxes, toy cars
instructions: 1. Challenge the child to build a "city" by stacking blocks as high as they can. 2. Use wider blocks at the base for stability. 3. Place toy cars on the "roofs" of the buildings. 4. Discuss why some towers fall and others stay standing. 5. Measure the height of the tallest building.

title: clipboarddisplay
instructions: 1. Mount a clipboard to a wall at the child's height. 2. Use the clip to display their latest drawing or project. 3. Rotate the artwork frequently to keep the "gallery" fresh. 4. Discuss the colors and shapes in the art currently on display. 5. This builds self-esteem and values their creative effort.

title: colourfeeders
what you'll need: Colored cardboard tubes, matching colored pom-poms
instructions: 1. Decorate cardboard tubes as "monsters" or "animals" of different colors. 2. Cut a "mouth" in each tube. 3. Have the child use a spoon or tweezers to "feed" the matching colored pom-poms to each animal. 4. Count how many pom-poms each animal ate. 5. Discuss which color was the most popular.

title: coloursampleart
what you'll need: Paint sample cards (from hardware store), glue, paper
instructions: 1. Collect a variety of paint sample cards in different hues. 2. Cut the cards into shapes or strips. 3. Glue the pieces onto paper to create a "gradient" artwork or a mosaic. 4. Arrange colors from lightest to darkest. 5. Discuss the names of the different colors (e.g., "Sky Blue" vs "Navy").

title: colourwalk
instructions: 1. Place different colored sheets of paper on the floor around the room. 2. Call out a color. 3. The child must walk, hop, or crawl to the matching paper. 4. Play music and have them "dance" from color to color. 5. Discuss the fastest way to get to each color.

title: countingpegs
instructions: 1. Create cards with numbers (1-10). 2. Have the child identify the number on the card. 3. Clip the matching number of pegs onto the edge of the card. 4. This builds the hand strength needed for writing. 5. Count the pegs once they are all attached.

title: customdice
what you'll need: Blank wooden cube or box, markers/stickers
instructions: 1. Draw different actions (jump, clap, spin) or numbers on each face of a cube. 2. Take turns rolling the die. 3. Everyone must perform the action shown. 4. If using numbers, the child must count out that many claps. 5. Discuss which side of the die comes up most often.

title: daisybloom
instructions: 1. Draw a daisy on paper and color it. 2. Fold the petals into the center to create a "bud." 3. Gently place the paper bud on the surface of a bowl of water. 4. Watch as the paper absorbs water and the flower "blooms" open. 5. Discuss how real flowers need water to open their petals.

title: dinobones
instructions: 1. Look at a picture of a dinosaur skeleton. 2. Use Q-tips as "bones." 3. Arrange and glue the Q-tips on black paper to recreate the skeleton. 4. Use half Q-tips for smaller bones like ribs or toes. 5. Discuss how scientists put real dinosaur bones back together.

title: dinomaze
instructions: 1. Use cardboard scraps to build a "maze" for a toy dinosaur. 2. Create dead ends and clear paths. 3. Guide the dinosaur through the maze to reach a "nest" at the end. 4. Use different heights of walls. 5. Discuss how the dinosaur might find its way out in the wild.

title: dinopatternblocks
instructions: 1. Provide a dinosaur outline filled with geometric shapes. 2. Have the child match real wooden or plastic shapes to the template. 3. Discuss the names of the shapes (triangle, hexagon, square). 4. Try to build a dinosaur from scratch using only the shapes. 5. Observe how different shapes fit together.

title: dinostretching
instructions: 1. Fold a paper dinosaur into a long accordion spring. 2. Tape one end to a table. 3. Pull the dinosaur's head and let go to watch it "stretch" and snap back. 4. Discuss how some dinosaurs had very long, flexible necks. 5. See how far you can stretch it before the tape peels.

title: doctortweezer
instructions: 1. Place small "bones" (beads) or "germs" (pom-poms) on a tray. 2. Provide the child with tweezers. 3. The child must "operate" by carefully removing the items and placing them in a bowl. 4. Discuss how doctors need very steady hands. 5. Time the "surgery" for an added challenge.

title: dropletsorting
instructions: 1. Fill a bowl with water and add a few drops of food coloring. 2. Use an eyedropper to pick up the "droplets." 3. Move the droplets into separate small containers or onto specific spots on a tray. 4. This builds the fine motor control needed for science experiments. 5. Count how many drops it takes to fill a small cap.

title: egghatch
what you'll need: Plastic eggs, toy chick or dino, water
instructions: 1. Place a toy inside a plastic egg. 2. Fill the egg with water and freeze it. 3. Provide the child with a "warm nest" (warm water and a salt shaker). 4. Use the salt and water to melt the ice and "hatch" the egg. 5. Discuss how birds and reptiles hatch from eggs.

title: elephantpour
instructions: 1. Fill a container with water. 2. Use an elephant-shaped pitcher or a funnel to "pour" water into smaller cups. 3. Try to fill the cups exactly to the "fill line" without spilling. 4. Discuss how much water the "elephant" can hold. 5. This is a great outdoor or bath-time activity.

title: exercisetoss
what you'll need: Cards with exercises (5 jumps, 3 spins), beanbag
instructions: 1. Toss a beanbag onto a grid of exercise cards. 2. Perform the exercise shown on the card where the beanbag lands. 3. Count out loud as you do each movement. 4. Discuss how exercise helps our muscles grow strong. 5. Take turns being the "trainer."

title: feedseagull
instructions: 1. Make a paper plate seagull with a large beak. 2. Provide several "fish" made of small clothespins. 3. Have the child clip the "fish" onto the seagull's beak to "feed" it. 4. Count the fish as they are caught. 5. Discuss what seagulls like to eat at the beach.

title: feedthefrog
what you'll need: Cardboard frog with a wide mouth, "flies" (pom-poms), tongs
instructions: 1. Decorate a cardboard box to look like a frog with a hole for a mouth. 2. Provide a bowl of "flies" (black pom-poms). 3. Use tongs or a large spoon to pick up the flies and drop them in the frog's mouth. 4. Count the flies as the frog eats. 5. Discuss how frogs use their long tongues to catch food.

title: find me
what you'll need: A "Find Me" checklist with pictures of objects in the room
instructions: 1. Give the child a list showing 5-10 items hidden in the room. 2. The child must search the room to find each item. 3. Check off each item as it is found. 4. Discuss where the items were hidden (e.g., "under the chair"). 5. Switch roles and have the child hide items for you.

title: findcars
what you'll need: Bowl of rice or sand, tiny toy cars
instructions: 1. Bury a specific number of tiny toy cars in a sensory bin. 2. Have the child dig through the bin to "find all the cars." 3. Line the cars up and count them to ensure none are left behind. 4. Discuss the colors of the cars found. 5. Sort the cars by size once they are all found.

title: finishpic
instructions: 1. Provide a page that has only half of a picture (e.g., half a face or half a house). 2. Ask the child to "finish the picture" by drawing the missing part. 3. Encourage them to use their imagination for the missing details. 4. Discuss why they chose to finish it that way. 5. This develops symmetry and creative thinking.

title: floating ghost
what you'll need: Balloon, tissue paper ghost, wool cloth
instructions: 1. Cut a small "ghost" out of lightweight tissue paper. 2. Rub a balloon against a wool cloth or your hair to build a charge. 3. Bring the balloon near the ghost without touching it. 4. Watch as the ghost "floats" up to meet the balloon. 5. Discuss how invisible static electricity can pull things.

title: foamwindowdots
instructions: 1. Dip foam "dots" or shapes into a bowl of water. 2. Press them against a window; they will stick to the glass! 3. Create patterns or pictures using the foam on the window. 4. Count how many dots you used. 5. When finished, simply peel them off—no mess!

title: fruitpuzzle
what you'll need: Pictures of fruit cut into 2 or 4 pieces
instructions: 1. Print pictures of different fruits (apple, banana, orange). 2. Cut each picture into segments like a puzzle. 3. Have the child reassemble the fruit. 4. Discuss how the pieces make a "whole" fruit. 5. Name the fruits and their colors.

title: geishagame
instructions: 1. Decorate a paper fan with traditional patterns. 2. Play a game where you must keep a feather or balloon in the air using only the "wind" from the fan. 3. Take turns and see who can keep it up the longest. 4. Discuss the history of fans in different cultures. 5. Practice "graceful" movements to the music.

title: germvisaulisation
instructions: 1. Apply a little lotion to hands and sprinkle with glitter ("germs"). 2. Have the child try to wipe them off with a dry towel (they won't budge!). 3. Try with just water. 4. Finally, use soap and warm water for 20 seconds. 5. Observe how the glitter finally disappears, just like real germs.

title: germ game
description: pretend to cough or sneeze and throw the pom poms to show who is "infected". Maybe when you infect them you draw a dot on their hand and they need to wash them. or you could use glitter to show how germs transfer.
instructions: 1. Pretend to "sneeze" and throw a handful of pom-poms toward a group. 2. Anyone touched by a pom-pom is "infected." 3. Draw a small dot on their hand with a washable marker. 4. The only way to remove the dot is to go to the "sink" and wash properly. 5. Discuss how covering our mouths stops germs from traveling.

title: habitatmatch
what you'll need: Animal cards, habitat cards (Jungle, Arctic, Desert)
instructions: 1. Lay out the different habitat cards. 2. Provide a bin of animal figures or cards. 3. Match each animal to its correct "home." 4. Discuss why a polar bear needs ice or a camel needs sand. 5. This builds an early understanding of environmental science.

title: habitats
what you'll need: Toy animals, natural materials (sand, water, leaves)
instructions: 1. Create mini-habitats using sensory bins (e.g., a bin with sand for the desert). 2. Place the correct toy animals in each bin. 3. Discuss what each animal eats and where it sleeps. 4. Move the animals between bins and discuss why they might not survive there. 5. This is great for open-ended imaginative play.

title: handcopy
instructions: 1. Paint the palm and fingers of one hand. 2. Press it firmly onto a sheet of paper. 3. Paint the other hand and press it next to the first one. 4. Observe the "copy" of your hands. 5. Count the fingers and compare the sizes.

title: jarcolourmatch
what you'll need: Glass jars, colored water, matching lids or items
instructions: 1. Fill jars with water dyed different colors. 2. Provide a bin of small items (beads, buttons) that match those colors. 3. Have the child drop the matching items into the correct colored jar. 4. Discuss how the items look under the water. 5. This is a calm, focused sensory activity.

title: jobmatch
what you'll need: Cards with people in different uniforms, tool cards
instructions: 1. Provide cards showing different jobs (Doctor, Firefighter, Chef). 2. Provide cards showing tools (Stethoscope, Hose, Whisk). 3. Match the tool to the person who uses it. 4. Discuss what you want to be when you grow up. 5. Act out the different jobs.

title: leafart
instructions: 1. Use collected leaves as the "body" for characters or animals. 2. Glue a leaf to paper and draw legs, arms, and a face around it. 3. Combine different leaf shapes to make a "leaf person." 4. Discuss the different textures (crunchy, soft) of the leaves. 5. This turns nature finds into imaginative art.

title: leafcounting
instructions: 1. Place stones with numbers (1-5) on the table. 2. Have the child place the matching number of leaves next to each stone. 3. Count the leaves out loud. 4. Discuss the colors and shapes of the leaves used. 5. This connects math to the natural world.

title: leafpatterns
instructions: 1. Place a leaf under a sheet of paper. 2. Rub a crayon over the paper to reveal the "veins" and patterns of the leaf. 3. Use different colors for different leaves. 4. Discuss how every leaf has a unique pattern, just like a fingerprint. 5. Cut out the rubbings to make a paper forest.

title: legoandpaper
instructions: 1. Challenge the child to build a bridge using only LEGO pillars and a single strip of paper. 2. See how much weight (pennies) the paper can hold. 3. Fold the paper into an accordion shape and try again. 4. Discuss why the folded paper is much stronger. 5. This is a classic introduction to structural engineering.

title: letterdice
instructions: 1. Write letters on the faces of a wooden cube. 2. Roll the die. 3. Say the name and sound of the letter that comes up. 4. Find an object in the room that starts with that letter. 5. This turns letter recognition into a fun game.

title: letterdraw
what you'll need: Tray of salt or sand, letter cards
instructions: 1. Show the child a letter card. 2. Have them "draw" that letter in the tray of salt using their finger. 3. Shake the tray to "erase" it and try a new letter. 4. This tactile feedback helps the brain remember letter shapes. 5. Practice drawing simple shapes like circles and squares too.

title: letterpegs
what you'll need: Clothespins (pegs) with letters, cardstock with names
instructions: 1. Write a child's name on a strip of cardstock. 2. Write the individual letters of the name on separate pegs. 3. The child must "clip" the pegs onto the card in the correct order to spell their name. 4. This builds hand strength and spelling skills. 5. Discuss the sounds of the letters as they are clipped.

title: lollystickpics
instructions: 1. Draw small characters or scenes on lolly sticks. 2. Arrange the sticks in different orders to tell a story. 3. Swap one stick for a new one to change the ending. 4. Discuss what happens next in the "lolly stick story." 5. This is a portable and endless storytelling tool.

title: lombardomethod
instructions: 1. Place a clear plastic sheet over a real object (like a toy or a leaf). 2. Use a marker to trace the outline of the object directly onto the plastic. 3. Lift the plastic to see the "copy." 4. Discuss how looking through the plastic helps you see the true shape. 5. This is a foundational technique for realistic drawing.

title: magnatilesnumberformation
instructions: 1. Write numbers (1-10) on Magna-Tiles. 2. Have the child arrange the tiles in order to form a long path. 3. Trace the numbers with a finger to practice number formation. 4. Use the tiles to build 3D numbered towers. 5. Wipe clean when finished.

title: makingpicturesbycuttingouttextures
instructions: 1. Search magazines for different textures (e.g., fur, water, brick). 2. Cut out the textures in specific shapes (like a circle for a sun or a triangle for a roof). 3. Glue the shapes together to create a "mixed-media" picture. 4. Discuss how the different textures feel to your eyes. 5. This develops visual literacy and scissor skills.

title: memoriseandcopy
what you'll need: Various small objects, a tray, a cloth
instructions: 1. Place 5 objects on a tray and let the child look for 10 seconds. 2. Cover the tray with a cloth. 3. Ask the child to name all the objects they remember. 4. Remove one object while they aren't looking and have them guess what is missing. 5. This significantly improves short-term memory and focus.

title: movingtv
what you'll need: Cardboard box, paper roll, two dowels
instructions: 1. Cut a "screen" out of a cardboard box. 2. Draw a series of scenes on a long roll of paper. 3. Tape the paper to the dowels inside the box. 4. Turn the dowels to "scroll" through the story on the TV screen. 5. Narrate the show for an audience.

title: netfishing
what you'll need: Small net (like a butterfly net), balls or toy fish
instructions: 1. Toss small items into the air or place them in a bin. 2. The child must use the net to "catch" the items. 3. Try catching a balloon for a slower-paced challenge. 4. Move the net quickly to catch "fast fish." 5. Discuss how fisherman use nets to catch food.

title: nocturnalanimals
what you'll need: Dark paper, white marker, nocturnal animal toys
instructions: 1. Discuss animals that are awake at night (Owls, Bats, Foxes). 2. Create a "night" scene on dark paper. 3. Place the nocturnal animals in the scene. 4. Discuss how they see in the dark (big eyes, sonar). 5. This builds an understanding of biological rhythms.

title: organmap
what you'll need: Large paper outline of a body, paper "organs"
instructions: 1. Trace the child's body on a large sheet of paper. 2. Provide cut-outs of the heart, lungs, and stomach. 3. Help the child place the organs in the correct spots on their "map." 4. Discuss what each organ does for the body. 5. This is a great introduction to human biology.

title: paintsmear
instructions: 1. Place a few drops of paint on paper. 2. Use a piece of cardboard to "smear" the paint across the surface. 3. Observe how the colors mix and create new streaks. 4. Move the cardboard in different directions (curvy, straight). 5. Discuss how the paint moves like a liquid.

title: paperchainskeleton
instructions: 1. Cut paper into strips and loops to create a "human" shape. 2. Use white strips for the "bones." 3. Connect the loops together to make a skeleton that can move. 4. Discuss how our bones are connected to help us move. 5. Hang the skeleton up for a fun decoration.

title: paperdrop
description: hold a piece of paper against a wall, over the child, drop it and see it they can catch it before it hits the ground
instructions: 1. Hold a piece of paper against the wall at the child's head height. 2. Without warning, let the paper go. 3. The child must try to "trap" the paper against the wall with their hands before it hits the floor. 4. Move the paper higher or lower to change the difficulty. 5. This develops fast reaction times and hand-eye coordination.

title: pentracing
what you'll need: Paper with printed lines or shapes, markers
instructions: 1. Provide a page with wavy, dashed, or dotted lines. 2. Have the child trace exactly over the lines with a marker. 3. Start with large, bold lines and move to smaller ones. 4. This builds the muscle memory needed for writing letters. 5. Use different colors to make it more engaging.

title: picasso
instructions: 1. Look at a portrait by Picasso. 2. Discuss how he moved the eyes and nose to different places. 3. Draw your own "Picasso" face by putting features where they don't usually go. 4. Use bold, bright colors. 5. Discuss how art doesn't always have to look "real" to be beautiful.

title: picture match
what you'll need: Photos of objects, matching real objects
instructions: 1. Take photos of 5 items in your house. 2. Show the child the photo. 3. They must race to find the real object and bring it back to the photo. 4. Discuss what the object is used for. 5. This connects digital images to the physical world.

title: playdoughanimals
what you'll need: Play dough, googly eyes, pipe cleaners
instructions: 1. Use play dough to create animal bodies. 2. Add pipe cleaners for legs and googly eyes for faces. 3. Discuss the different animals you are making. 4. Squash the animals and make new ones! 5. This is great for open-ended creative play.

title: playdoughconstellations
instructions: 1. Flatten a piece of play dough. 2. Look at a picture of a constellation (like the Big Dipper). 3. Use toothpicks to mark where the stars are in the dough. 4. Connect the toothpicks with string to see the shape. 5. Discuss how people see pictures in the stars at night.

title: playdoughdinos
instructions: 1. Create a "prehistoric world" using play dough and stones. 2. Place dinosaurs in the scene. 3. Press the dinosaurs into the dough to make tracks. 4. Discuss what dinosaurs might have eaten. 5. Use the scene for imaginative play.

title: playdoughdinos2
instructions: 1. Give the child a lump of play dough. 2. Ask them to "copy" a toy dinosaur by modeling one out of dough. 3. Focus on the long neck or the sharp spikes. 4. Discuss how the play dough version is different from the plastic one. 5. This builds observation skills and fine motor control.

title: playdoughdinos3
instructions: 1. Give the child a lump of play dough. 2. Ask them to "copy" a toy dinosaur by modeling one out of dough. 3. Focus on the long neck or the sharp spikes. 4. Discuss how the play dough version is different from the plastic one. 5. This builds observation skills and fine motor control.

title: playdoughdinos4
instructions: 1. Give the child a lump of play dough. 2. Ask them to "copy" a toy dinosaur by modeling one out of dough. 3. Focus on the long neck or the sharp spikes. 4. Discuss how the play dough version is different from the plastic one. 5. This builds observation skills and fine motor control.

title: playdoughfruit
what you'll need: Play dough, plastic fruit molds or toys
instructions: 1. Roll out play dough and use molds to make "fruit." 2. Sort the dough fruit by color. 3. Count how many apples or bananas you made. 4. "Slice" the fruit using a plastic knife. 5. Discuss the different types of fruit we eat.

title: playdoughorgans
instructions: 1. Provide a outline of a torso. 2. Use different colors of play dough to model the heart, lungs, and stomach. 3. Place the dough organs on the template. 4. Discuss what each organ does. 5. This is a tactile way to learn about the inside of our bodies.

title: playdoughshapes
instructions: 1. Roll out play dough into a flat sheet. 2. Use cookie cutters to cut out circles, squares, and triangles. 3. Identify the shapes as you cut them. 4. Combine the shapes to make a "play dough house." 5. Count how many sides each shape has.

title: playdoughxmas
what you'll need: Play dough, glitter, small star or tree cutters
instructions: 1. Mix glitter into green or red play dough. 2. Use cutters to make stars or trees. 3. Decorate the dough with small beads. 4. Discuss holiday traditions while you play. 5. This is a festive and tactile sensory activity.

title: pompomgoal
instructions: 1. Set up small "goals" made of cardboard on a table. 2. Place a pom-pom in the center. 3. Use a straw to blow air at the pom-pom to move it. 4. Try to "score" a goal by blowing the pom-pom into the net. 5. This builds breath control and coordination.

title: pompompatterns
instructions: 1. Provide cards showing a sequence of colors (e.g., Yellow-Green-Yellow). 2. Have the child place matching pom-poms onto the card. 3. Try to continue the pattern without the card. 4. Discuss what color comes next. 5. This develops foundational logic for math and coding.

title: potrecipe
instructions: 1. Provide a "recipe card" with pictures (e.g., 3 blue blocks, 2 red pom-poms). 2. Have the child find the items and "add" them to the pot. 3. Stir the "soup" with a large spoon. 4. Count the items as they go in. 5. This integrates counting with roleplay.

title: ramp
what you'll need: Cardboard plank, toy cars, different surfaces
instructions: 1. Prop up one end of a board to make a ramp. 2. Roll a car down and measure how far it goes. 3. Cover the ramp with a towel and try again. 4. Discuss why the car goes slower on the towel (friction). 5. Try making the ramp steeper to see if the car goes faster.

title: recycling
instructions: 1. Provide a mix of plastic, paper, and metal items. 2. Sort the items into the correct bins. 3. Discuss how we can reuse some items for art (junk modeling). 4. Identify the recycling symbol on packages. 5. Talk about how recycling helps the Earth.

title: rhymingpairs
what you'll need: Cards with pictures of rhyming words (Cat/Hat, Dog/Log)
instructions: 1. Lay the cards face down in a grid. 2. Take turns flipping two cards. 3. If the words rhyme, keep the pair. 4. Say the words out loud to hear the matching sounds. 5. This builds phonemic awareness needed for reading.

title: robothand
instructions: 1. Trace a hand on cardboard and cut it out. 2. Tape straw segments to the fingers. 3. Thread string through the straws. 4. Pull the strings to make the cardboard fingers "curse" and grab. 5. Discuss how our own muscles and tendons help our hands move.

title: sandshapes
instructions: 1. Glue cardboard shapes (circle, square) onto a piece of cardstock. 2. Apply glue inside the shapes. 3. Sprinkle sand over the glue. 4. Once dry, have the child close their eyes and feel the "sand shapes." 5. Discuss the names and textures of the shapes.

title: sandwhichbuild
what you'll need: Play dough, plastic knife, paper plates
instructions: 1. Roll out play dough into "bread" and "filling" layers. 2. Stack the layers to build a "sandwich." 3. Use a plastic knife to cut the sandwich in half or quarters. 4. Discuss how the pieces make a whole sandwich. 5. Count the layers as you build them.

title: santatrails
instructions: 1. Draw a path for "Santa" on a sheet of paper. 2. Use stickers or stamps to mark the "trail." 3. Add obstacles like "snow drifts" (cotton balls). 4. Guide a toy sleigh along the path. 5. Discuss the tradition of Santa's journey while you play.

title: sensematch
what you'll need: Objects for different senses (lemon for taste, bell for sound)
instructions: 1. Set out a series of items. 2. Match each item to a card representing the sense used to experience it (e.g., a flower matches the "nose" card). 3. Discuss which sense is your favorite. 4. Try a "blindfold" challenge to see if you can guess the item using only touch or smell. 5. This builds awareness of how our bodies perceive the world.

title: sensory toolkit.pdf
what you'll need: PDF guide or curated box of textures, scents, and sounds
instructions: 1. Provide a variety of tools like stress balls, scented sachets, and music. 2. Have the child explore the different items. 3. Discuss which items make them feel "calm" or "happy." 4. Use the toolkit as a resource for self-regulation. 5. This develops emotional intelligence and sensory awareness.

title: shapedeconstruction
instructions: 1. Provide a large shape (like a big house) made of smaller shapes. 2. "Deconstruct" the house by removing the triangles and squares. 3. Try to put it back together like a puzzle. 4. Discuss how big shapes are often made of smaller ones. 5. Create a new image using the same pieces.

title: shapematch
what you'll need: Objects of different shapes, matching cards
instructions: 1. Lay out cards with a circle, square, and triangle. 2. Find objects in the room that match the shapes on the cards (e.g., a clock for a circle). 3. Place the object on the matching card. 4. Discuss the properties of the shapes (e.g., "This one has 3 sides"). 5. This connects geometry to everyday life.

title: shapesort
what you'll need: Bin of mixed blocks or toys, sorting trays
instructions: 1. Dump out a bin of mixed items. 2. Sort the items by shape (all circles here, all squares there). 3. Count how many of each shape you found. 4. Discuss which shape was the most common. 5. This is a foundational skill for organization and math.

title: shopcount
instructions: 1. Set up a "shop" with items and price tags (1, 2, 3). 2. Have the child "buy" items and count out the coins needed. 3. Count the items in the basket at the "checkout." 4. Practice basic addition by buying two items. 5. This turns math into a fun social game.

title: shopmatch
instructions: 1. Set out a shelf with different "departments" (e.g., Fruit, Bakery). 2. Have the child place the toy food in the correct section. 3. Discuss why milk goes in the fridge and bread on the shelf. 4. This develops categorization skills and environmental awareness. 5. Roleplay being the shopkeeper.

title: shoppinglist
what you'll need: Shopping list with pictures and numbers
instructions: 1. Give the child a list (e.g., 2 apples, 1 milk). 2. They must navigate the "shop" to find exactly what is on the list. 3. Check items off as they are found. 4. Discuss the quantities needed. 5. This integrates reading, counting, and focus.

title: sickteddycount
instructions: 1. Place a "sick" teddy in a bed with several "ailments" (dots). 2. Have the child count how many spots the teddy has. 3. "Prescribe" a number of beads as medicine. 4. Count the beads into a small cup. 5. Discuss how to be kind and helpful to those who are unwell.

title: sightwordswat
instructions: 1. Lay out sight word cards on the table or floor. 2. Call out a word. 3. The child must race to "swat" the correct word with a fly swatter. 4. This turns reading practice into a high-energy game. 5. See how many words you can swat in one minute.

title: smoothierecipes
what you'll need: Blender, various fruits, milk/yogurt, printed recipe
instructions: 1. Provide a recipe card with pictures of the ingredients (e.g., 5 strawberries, 1 banana). 2. Have the child count out the ingredients and add them to the blender. 3. Help the child press the buttons to blend the smoothie. 4. Discuss the colors of the fruits as they mix. 5. Pour and enjoy the healthy snack you made together.

title: snailtracing
instructions: 1. Draw a large spiral on a piece of paper to represent a snail's shell. 2. Place a small toy snail or button at the start of the line. 3. Have the child trace the spiral slowly with a marker. 4. Encourage them to stay on the line to "help the snail home." 5. Add "grass" and "flowers" around the snail once finished.

title: splitpinsolarsystem
what you'll need: Paper planets, cardstock sun, split pins (brass fasteners)
instructions: 1. Cut out circles of different sizes to represent the planets and a large sun. 2. Punch a hole at the end of a thin strip of cardstock for each planet. 3. Use split pins to attach the planet strips to the central sun. 4. Rotate the planets around the sun to show how they orbit. 5. Discuss the names and order of the planets in our solar system.

title: staticdancers
instructions: 1. Cut small human shapes out of lightweight tissue paper. 2. Rub a balloon against a wool cloth or your hair to build a charge. 3. Hold the balloon over the paper dancers. 4. Watch as the dancers "jump" and dance toward the balloon. 5. Discuss how invisible static electricity can move objects.

title: stonespelling
instructions: 1. Write individual letters on smooth stones. 2. Provide a word card (e.g., "CAT" or "DOG"). 3. Have the child find the matching letter stones and arrange them to spell the word. 4. Use the stones to practice the child's name. 5. This tactile way of spelling makes learning letters more engaging.

title: suitcase
what you'll need: Small suitcase or bag, clothes, travel photos
instructions: 1. Discuss where you might go on a holiday (beach, mountains). 2. Provide a small suitcase and a pile of clothes. 3. Ask the child to "pack" what they would need for that specific trip. 4. Use photos of the destination to prompt their choices. 5. Roleplay the journey from the house to the airport or train station.

title: tape colour match
what you'll need: Different colors of tape, matching colored toys
instructions: 1. Place strips of different colored tape on a table or floor. 2. Have the child find objects in the house that match each tape color. 3. Place the objects on the corresponding tape line. 4. Count how many items were found for each color. 5. Discuss which color was the easiest to find.

title: teariffic art
what you'll need: Paper, glue, scraps of colored paper
instructions: 1. Draw a simple shape or animal on a piece of paper. 2. Have the child "tear" colorful paper into small bits (this builds hand strength). 3. Apply glue to the drawing. 4. Cover the drawing with the torn paper scraps to create a textured collage. 5. Discuss the "tear-iffic" patterns created by the rough edges.

title: toolbox shapes
what you'll need: Cardboard "toolbox," paper tools in different shapes
instructions: 1. Create a cardboard toolbox with slots labeled with shapes (Circle, Square, Triangle). 2. Cut "tools" out of paper in those specific shapes (e.g., a circular saw, a triangular wedge). 3. Have the child sort the tools into the correct slots in the toolbox. 4. Discuss the names and sides of each shape. 5. Roleplay being a builder fixing things around the room.

title: unbolted
what you'll need: Nuts, bolts, washers, wood block with holes
instructions: 1. Provide a set of real nuts and bolts. 2. Have the child practice twisting the nuts onto the bolts until they are secure. 3. "Unbolt" them to start over. 4. Use a wrench if available to show how tools make the job easier. 5. This develops the rotational hand movement needed for many life skills.

title: unnamed (82)
instructions: 1. Squirt a layer of shaving cream onto a tray. 2. Add drops of different colored paint. 3. Use a stick or finger to "swirl" the colors into the cream. 4. Press a piece of paper onto the surface to take a "print" of the pattern. 5. Scrape off the excess cream to reveal a marbled masterpiece.

title: untangle
what you'll need: Mixed lengths of yarn or string, beads
instructions: 1. Create a "tangle" of colorful yarn. 2. Have the child carefully pull the strings apart to "untangle" them. 3. To add a challenge, thread a bead onto each string that must be moved to the end. 4. Discuss being patient while solving a tricky problem. 5. Use the untangled strings to make a giant "web" in the room.

title: vehicle place
what you'll need: Play mat with roads/water/sky, toy vehicles
instructions: 1. Provide a mat or drawing showing land, sea, and air. 2. Give the child a variety of toy vehicles (boat, car, plane). 3. Have the child "place" each vehicle in its correct environment. 4. Discuss why a bus stays on the road and a boat stays in the water. 5. Roleplay a long journey using all three types of transport.

title: very hungry caterpillar count and thread
instructions: 1. Look at "The Very Hungry Caterpillar" story. 2. Create a caterpillar head and several paper leaves with a hole in the middle. 3. Write numbers on the leaves. 4. Have the child "thread" the caterpillar through the leaves in numerical order. 5. Count the leaves as the caterpillar "eats" through them.

title: washingline
instructions: 1. Tie a string between two chairs at child-height. 2. Provide a basket of small clothes and pegs. 3. Have the child hang the clothes on the line using the pegs. 4. Count how many items are on the line. 5. This builds the hand strength and coordination needed for daily self-care.

title: waterfilter
what you'll need: Plastic bottle, sand, gravel, charcoal, dirty water
instructions: 1. Cut a plastic bottle in half and flip the top into the bottom like a funnel. 2. Layer gravel, sand, and charcoal inside. 3. Pour "dirty" water (water mixed with dirt) into the top. 4. Observe as the water drips through the layers and comes out cleaner at the bottom. 5. Discuss why it is important to have clean water to drink.

title: watermelon counting
instructions: 1. Cut red paper triangles and add a green "rind" edge. 2. Write a number on the rind. 3. Have the child place that exact number of black beans or seeds onto the red part. 4. Count the seeds out loud. 5. Discuss the colors and shape of the watermelon.

title: windowsticks
what you'll need: Contact paper (sticky back plastic), window, tissue paper
instructions: 1. Tape a piece of contact paper to a window with the sticky side facing out. 2. Provide a variety of colorful tissue paper shapes. 3. Have the child press the shapes onto the window to create a "stained glass" effect. 4. Watch how the sunlight shines through the colors. 5. Peel off and rearrange to create new designs.

title: salt volcano
what you'll need: Salt, food coloring, tray, liquid glue
instructions: 1. Draw a "volcano" shape on a tray using liquid glue. 2. Sprinkle a thick layer of salt over the glue. 3. Use an eyedropper to drop colored water onto the salt. 4. Watch as the salt absorbs the color and "erupts" along the glue lines. 5. Discuss how the salt pulls the water in through capillary action.

title: pie recipes
what you'll need: Printed pie recipe, play dough, pie dish
instructions: 1. Look at a simple pie recipe with pictures. 2. Use play dough to "make" the pie, counting the layers of crust and filling. 3. "Slice" the finished pie into quarters. 4. Discuss the steps of baking (mixing, rolling, heating). 5. Roleplay serving the pie to friends in a "bakery."

title: cork boats
what you'll need: Corks, rubber bands, toothpicks, paper (for sails)
instructions: 1. Bundle three corks together using rubber bands to create a raft. 2. Stick a toothpick into the center cork for a mast. 3. Add a small paper sail. 4. Place the boat in a tub of water to see if it floats. 5. Blow on the sail to race it across the "pond."

title: tantrix
description: a game where you use these hexagonial tiles to try to make the longest loop or line of your chosen colour
instructions: 1. Provide a set of tiles with colored paths. 2. Choose one color (e.g., Red). 3. Take turns adding tiles to build the longest continuous line or loop of your color. 4. Ensure the colors on the edges of the tiles match up. 5. This develops strategic thinking and pattern recognition.

title: spring flower scavenger hunt
what you'll need: Scavenger hunt list with spring flowers
instructions: 1. Take a printed list of local spring flowers (Daffodil, Bluebell, Primrose) on a walk. 2. Search the park or garden to find each one. 3. Tick the flower off the list once found. 4. Discuss the different colors and shapes of the petals. 5. Remember to observe only—do not pick the wild flowers!

title: spring nature scavenger hunt
what you'll need: List of "nature treasures" (feather, smooth stone, twig)
instructions: 1. Go on a nature walk with a scavenger hunt list. 2. Search for items of different textures and colors. 3. Collect the "treasures" in a small bag. 4. Discuss where each item was found (e.g., "The feather was near the pond"). 5. Use the treasures to make a nature collage back at home.

title: spring woodland wildlife scavenger hunt
what you'll need: List of woodland animals (Squirrel, Woodpecker, Beetle)
instructions: 1. Walk through a wooded area with your checklist. 2. Look up in the trees and down under logs for wildlife. 3. Check off the animals or signs of animals (like a nest or nuts) that you find. 4. Discuss how the animals use the trees for shelter. 5. This builds an early awareness of ecosystems.

title: making compost
what you'll need: Organic waste (veg peels), soil, large bin/jar
instructions: 1. Place a layer of soil in a container. 2. Add organic kitchen scraps like fruit peels or eggshells. 3. Add another layer of soil and a little water. 4. Stir occasionally and observe over several weeks as the scraps disappear. 5. Discuss how "compost" turns waste into food for new plants.

title: ideas for active physical play indoors
instructions: 1. Use masking tape to create "hopscotch" or paths on the carpet. 2. Build an "obstacle course" using pillows to jump over and chairs to crawl under. 3. Set up a "bowling alley" with empty plastic bottles. 4. This keeps children active and burning energy even when they can't go outside. 5. Time the course for a fun challenge.

title: learn about schemas (for parents)
description: observe your children and see what you can do to encourage whatever schemas they are displaying
instructions: 1. Read about common schemas (patterns of behavior) like "Transporting" or "Enveloping." 2. Observe your child playing and see if you notice these repeating patterns. 3. Provide materials that support their current schema (e.g., if they like "Connecting," provide tape and string). 4. This helps you understand how your child is learning through play. 5. Share your observations with other caregivers.

title: frugal fun 4 boys and girls
description: resource with lots of activities
what you'll need: Frugal Fun 4 Boys and Girls website
instructions: 1. Browse the website for low-cost, high-engagement STEM and art projects. 2. Select an activity based on the materials you already have at home. 3. Follow the step-by-step guides to build a project with your child. 4. Use the "Ages 3-5" section for developmentally appropriate ideas. 5. This is a great resource for "frugal" educational fun.

title: fish bite
instructions: 1. Color a clothespin to look like a large fish or shark. 2. Cut a small paper "worm" or "smaller fish." 3. Squeeze the clothespin to make the "big fish" open its mouth. 4. Have the big fish "bite" and hold the smaller one. 5. This builds the hand muscles needed for advanced scissor work and writing.

title: musical poses
instructions: 1. Play music and have the children dance or move around. 2. When the music stops, call out a "pose" (e.g., "Pose like a tree!" or "Pose like a frog!"). 3. Everyone must freeze in that specific shape. 4. Discuss how our muscles help us stay very still. 5. Use different speeds of music to change the energy of the poses.

title: one little project
description: resource with lots of ideas
instructions: 1. Explore the website for creative crafts and easy-to-follow art tutorials. 2. Pick a "project of the week" to do together. 3. Gather the simple materials listed (usually household items). 4. Follow the photo-based instructions to create something new. 5. This provides a steady stream of fresh ideas for home-based learning.

title: sussex wildlife trust events
instructions: 1. Check the website for local nature events, workshops, and guided walks. 2. Plan a visit to a nearby reserve based on their suggestions. 3. Participate in a "Wild Beach" or "Forest School" session if available. 4. Use their seasonal guides to know what to look for in nature this month. 5. This connects your family to local conservation efforts.

title: constructing 3d models based on pictures
instructions: 1. Provide a set of building blocks (cubes, prisms). 2. Show the child a photo of a simple 3D model (e.g., a tower or a small house). 3. Challenge the child to recreate the model exactly as it looks in the photo. 4. Discuss which shapes are at the bottom and which are at the top. 5. This builds foundational skills for geometry and engineering.

title: words for life
description: A collection of resources relating to literacy
instructions: 1. Explore the resources for age-appropriate literacy activities (Age 3-4). 2. Use their tips for storytelling and reading aloud. 3. Try one of the suggested "word games" to build vocabulary. 4. Access their milestone guides to track your child's speech development. 5. This supports the foundational "words for life" needed for success in school.

title: learn about different religions
instructions: 1. Watch short videos about different religious festivals and traditions. 2. Discuss how people around the world celebrate in different ways. 3. Look at photos of places of worship (Mosques, Churches, Temples). 4. Talk about the values shared across different beliefs, like kindness and charity. 5. This builds a broad, respectful understanding of the global community.

title: the exploratory
description: a resource for science based activities
instructions: 1. Browse the "snacks" for simple, bite-sized science experiments. 2. Choose a "physics" or "light" activity using kitchen materials. 3. Ask your child "What do you think will happen?" before starting. 4. Conduct the experiment and observe the results together. 5. This turns your home into a laboratory for exploration.

title: flying plastic
what you'll need: Plastic produce bag (very light), fan or hair dryer
instructions: 1. Open a very lightweight plastic bag (like a fruit bag from the shop). 2. Use a fan or hair dryer on a cool setting to blow air underneath it. 3. Watch as the bag "flies" and hovers in the air stream. 4. Move the fan to see if you can guide the bag around the room. 5. Discuss how air can push and lift light objects.

title: Phenakistoscope
description: make moving pictures by spinning
instructions: 1. Draw a series of slightly different images around the edge of a cardboard disk. 2. Poke a hole in the center and insert a skewer or pencil. 3. Spin the disk rapidly while looking into a mirror through the slits in the disk. 4. The images will appear to "move" like a movie. 5. This is the "Phenakistoscope," one of the first ways humans made animations.
variations: try a horizontal version by making it more like a spinning top, maybe using a pencil

title: ways to help wildlife at home
instructions: 1. Explore the "Actions" section for ways to help nature at home (e.g., building a bug hotel). 2. Pick one project to complete in your garden or on your balcony. 3. Track the results—do you see more bees or birds visiting? 4. Discuss why helping wildlife is important for a healthy planet. 5. This empowers children to take positive environmental action.

title: ID guides
description: wildlife trust species identification guides
instructions: 1. Use the ID guides (online or printed) to identify birds, butterflies, or trees in your area. 2. Take the guide outside and see how many species you can find. 3. Look for specific features mentioned in the guide (e.g., "red breast" or "jagged leaf"). 4. Discuss how having a name for things helps us notice them more. 5. Start a "species list" for your garden.

title: wildlife watch things to do
instructions: 1. Look for "Things to Do" on the website, such as birdwatching or pond dipping. 2. Follow the guides to conduct your own nature survey. 3. Upload your findings if the site has a citizen science project running. 4. Learn about local wildlife through their interactive games. 5. This builds a lifelong connection to the natural world.

title: ideas for active physical play
instructions: 1. Use the PDF cards for ideas on active physical play (e.g., skipping, balancing). 2. Set up a "Daily Mile" or a short movement challenge. 3. Focus on a different skill each day (Agility, Balance, Coordination). 4. Use household items as "sports equipment." 5. This helps maintain physical health and motor development at home.

title: cosmic kids yoga
description: kids yoga videos with themes like animals, dinosaurs, disney and minecraft
instructions: 1. Choose a themed yoga video (e.g., Frozen, Minecraft, or Dinosaurs). 2. Follow along with the story-based poses. 3. Practice "mindfulness" and stretching in a fun, engaging way. 4. Use the breathing exercises to help with "calm down" time. 5. This integrates physical exercise with imaginative storytelling.

title: simple breathing exercise with cat animation
instructions: 1. Watch the animation of the cat breathing in and out. 2. Have the child match their own breathing to the movement of the cat. 3. Breathe in slowly through the nose as the cat expands, and out through the mouth as it shrinks. 4. Use this as a "reset" tool when the child feels frustrated or over-excited. 5. This develops foundational skills for emotional regulation.

title: runaround game show quiz
instructions: 1. Set up a "quiz" where the child must run to different areas of the room for "True" or "False" answers. 2. Ask questions about things they have learned (e.g., "Do ducks have four legs?"). 3. The high-energy movement makes learning feel like a game show. 4. Take turns being the "Host." 5. This builds confidence in expressing knowledge.
info checked: ask a multiple choice question, the children have 15 seconds to run to a designated spot that represents one of the answers, the question is repeated and they have another 15 seconds if they want to change their minds, the answer is revealed

title: transport water from one container to another using only a cloth or sponge  by wringing it out
what you'll need: Two containers, sponge or cloth, water
instructions: 1. Fill one container with water and leave the second one empty. 2. Give the child a sponge or a thick cloth. 3. The goal is to move all the water from the first container to the second using *only* the sponge. 4. Soak up the water, then "wring" it out into the new container. 5. Discuss how the sponge "holds" the water.

title: water pistols or spray bottles
description: could put shaving foam or bubbles on an outside window and see if they can knock it off or pop. Could also see if they can clean dirty dishes.
what you'll need: Water pistols or spray bottles, bubbles/foam
instructions: 1. Squirt shaving foam or bubbles onto an outside window. 2. Have the child use a water pistol or spray bottle to "knock off" the foam. 3. Try to hit specific targets or pop the bubbles. 4. Use the spray bottle to "clean" dirty dishes or toys. 5. This strengthens the finger muscles used for writing.

title: scissor skills in the kitchen
description: see which jobs in the kitchen can be done by your child to devlop their scissor skills e.g. opening packaging, cutting slices of pizza, cutting green beans, rolling up lettuce leaves and cuttingthem into strips.
instructions: 1. Identify safe "cutting" jobs in the kitchen (e.g., snipping green beans, cutting pizza slices). 2. Have the child help open food packaging using scissors. 3. Roll up lettuce leaves and have the child cut them into thin "ribbons." 4. This builds real-world scissor skills in a meaningful context. 5. Always supervise closely during kitchen activities.

title: clap game
description: have the child sit in front of you, clap a simple rhythm and see if they can copy it
instructions: 1. Sit facing the child. 2. Clap a very simple rhythm (e.g., Clap-Clap-Pause-Clap). 3. The child must try to "copycat" the rhythm exactly. 4. Gradually make the rhythms more complex as they get better. 5. This develops the listening skills and auditory memory needed for language.

title: table roll
description: put a table or something at an angle and roll objects down, the child catches the items in a basket as they fall
what you'll need: Tilted table or plank, basket, balls/toys
instructions: 1. Prop up one end of a table or board to create a steep ramp. 2. Roll objects down the ramp one by one. 3. The child must stand at the bottom and "catch" the objects in a basket before they hit the floor. 4. Vary the speed by changing the angle of the ramp. 5. Discuss why heavier or rounder objects might roll faster.

title: cup catch
description: roll marbles or balls and see it your child can catch them under a cup
what you'll need: Plastic cup, small balls or marbles
instructions: 1. Roll a ball across the floor toward the child. 2. The child must move their cup to "trap" the ball under it as it rolls past. 3. Try rolling the ball at different speeds. 4. Practice "aiming" the cup to catch the ball. 5. This develops fast reaction times and hand-eye coordination.

title: tissue drop
description: drop a tissue or light scraf from up high and see if they can catch it before it hits the ground, could be done with any light, floaty object e.g. feather
instructions: 1. Hold a tissue or scarf up as high as you can. 2. Let it go and watch it float down. 3. The child must try to "catch" it with their hands before it touches the ground. 4. Discuss why the tissue falls slowly and "wiggles" through the air. 5. Try catching it with different body parts (e.g., "Catch it with your head!").

title: Materials game:
description: write a material on a sticky pad and ask the kids to stick it on something made of that material. Or if outside say to go touch something, inside ask them to bring something made of that material
instructions: 1. Write a material name (e.g., "Wood," "Plastic," "Metal") on a sticky note. 2. Have the child go around the house and stick the note on something made of that material. 3. If outside, play a "Touch Game"—say "Go touch something made of stone!" 4. Discuss how each material feels (cold, hard, smooth). 5. This builds an early understanding of material properties.

title: Robot game:
description: I am a robot, if I catch you you become robot and turn other humans into robot, robots do not run and you have to move and talk like a robot
instructions: 1. The "Lead Robot" (parent) tries to catch the "Humans." 2. If caught, the human becomes a robot too. 3. Important rule: Robots cannot run—they must move with stiff, mechanical limbs and talk in a robot voice. 4. The game ends when everyone has been "upgraded" to a robot. 5. This encourages creative movement and follows a fun social narrative.

title: acting out 5 little ducks
description: sing 5 little ducks went swimming one day, pretend to swim while walking away for "swimming one day", have some kind of obstacle to go over for "over the hill", run as far away as you can for "far away", do it all in reverse for "ducks came back"
instructions: 1. Sing "Five Little Ducks Went Swimming One Day." 2. Act out the movements: "Swimming" (walking and waving arms), "Over the hill" (stepping over a pillow). 3. Have the "ducks" run as far away as they can for "Far away." 4. Do the whole sequence in reverse when the ducks "come back." 5. This links rhythm and rhyme to physical memory.

title: word puzzles
description: print or write a nursery rhyme your child knows by heart, cut out each word, sentences or phrases and see if they can put it all back together in the right order. encourage them tosound out the words.
instructions: 1. Print out a favorite nursery rhyme (e.g., Twinkle Twinkle). 2. Cut the rhyme into individual words or sentences. 3. Mix them up and have the child try to put the rhyme back together in the correct order. 4. Encourage them to "sound out" the words they recognize. 5. This develops reading comprehension and sequencing skills.

title: learn about our coasts
description: https://dnu7gk7p9afoo.cloudfront.net/Files/wcs-family-coastal-trail-bookletwebfinal.pdf
instructions: 1. Use the booklet to learn about the animals and plants found at the British seaside. 2. If visiting the coast, use the trail map to find specific landmarks. 3. Discuss how the tide moves in and out. 4. Look for "beach treasures" like sea glass or shells. 5. This builds an appreciation for coastal ecosystems.

title: wildlife ID guides
description: https://www.discoverthewild.co.uk/resources
instructions: 1. Explore the ID guides for fungi, wildflowers, or insects. 2. Use the guides to help name the things you see in your local park. 3. Discuss the "clues" that help you identify a species (e.g., the number of spots on a ladybird). 4. This turns a simple walk into a scientific expedition. 5. Start a nature journal using the names you've learned.

title: leaf art
description: go on a walk, collect some leaves and arrange them to make a picture
instructions: 1. Go on a walk and collect leaves of many different shapes and sizes. 2. Arrange the leaves on a piece of paper to "build" a picture (e.g., a leaf owl or a leaf car). 3. Glue the leaves down once you are happy with the design. 4. Add details with markers once the glue is dry. 5. Discuss the different colors of the leaves (Green, Yellow, Brown).

title: Yoghurt cake recipe for counting,
what you'll need: Yogurt pot, cake ingredients (flour, sugar, eggs)
instructions: 1. Use an empty yogurt pot as your only measuring tool (the "pot method"). 2. Follow a simple recipe: e.g., 1 pot of yogurt, 2 pots of sugar, 3 pots of flour. 3. Have the child count out the pots of each ingredient. 4. Mix together and bake. 5. This teaches ratios and counting in a delicious way.

title: Fill a stuffed animal with rice to make a weighted doll
instructions: 1. Carefully open a small seam on a stuffed animal. 2. Replace some of the stuffing with a bag of dry rice. 3. Sew the seam back up securely. 4. The extra weight provides "deep pressure" input when the child holds the doll. 5. This can be a very calming tool for children who enjoy sensory grounding.

title: beach card:
description: glue sand onto beach part, put water dyed blue in a bag
what you'll need: Cardstock, sand, glue, Ziploc bag, blue water
instructions: 1. Glue sand to the bottom half of a card to make a "beach." 2. Fill a small Ziploc bag with water dyed blue. 3. Tape the bag to the top half of the card to create a "liquid ocean." 4. The child can squish the water to see the "waves" move above the sand. 5. Discuss what animals might live in the water or on the beach.

title: just dance videos
description: search just dance videos on youtube and follow along, you can check if they have your childs favourite songs
instructions: 1. Search for "Just Dance Kids" on YouTube. 2. Choose a song the child loves. 3. Follow the movements of the characters on the screen. 4. This is a high-energy way to practice following sequences and rhythm. 5. Have a "dance-off" to see who can mirror the moves best.

title: karaoke
description: find karaoke versions of your childs favurite songs on youtube
instructions: 1. Find the "karaoke" or "instrumental with lyrics" version of a favorite song. 2. Use a hairbrush as a microphone. 3. Sing along to the music. 4. This builds confidence in performance and helps with word recognition. 5. Discuss the "story" being told in the song.

title: snap
description: practise subetising (knowing how many of something there is without needing to count, you could cover up the numbers with masking tape if you want to make sure they're not just reading them)
what you'll need: Standard deck of cards (or number cards)
instructions: 1. Play a game of "Snap" where you match numbers. 2. Challenge: Instead of reading the digit, try to "know" the number of pips/dots just by looking (subitizing). 3. You can cover the digits with tape to force focus on the patterns. 4. This builds the foundational speed for mental math. 5. The first person to "Snap" the matching pattern wins the pile.

title: subetising game
description: show your child a number of items between 1 and 10 but only reveal them breifly or get them to close their eyes and only look briefly. the aim is to know how many there are without needing to count, show them for more or less time depending on how long they need.
instructions: 1. Place a few items on the table. 2. Reveal them for only 2 seconds, then cover them with the cloth. 3. Ask the child "How many did you see?" without letting them count one-by-one. 4. Start with 1-3 items and increase as they get faster. 5. This strengthens the brain's ability to see groups of numbers instantly.

title: write dance
description: put on a piece of music and ask your child to draw to the beat, see how different types of music look e.g. classical, jazz, EDM, or share instrumental versions of your favourite songs. Try as many different genres as you can find but try and avoid anything with lyrics as you are trying to get them to react to just the sounds
what you'll need: Paper, markers, different genres of music
instructions: 1. Put on a piece of music (Classical, Jazz, or EDM). 2. Use instrumental versions to avoid lyrics. 3. Ask the child to "draw the sound" using markers. 4. High, fast music might lead to dots and zigzags; slow, low music might lead to long, wavy lines. 5. Compare the drawings for each genre to see how the music "looks."

title: adaptation game
description: show your child a picture of an  animal in its natural habitat and ask why they think they might have certain features. Don't lead them towards the correct answer, you're trying to develop their thinking skills so any answer that comes from any line of reasoning is good. But if they want to know after they have made their guess and explained why you can look it up together and discuss. after you've done a few you could give them a habitat and get them to draw what kind of animal would live there and help them label the different features. You could also give them an animal and have them guess where it might live based on its features or give them a few cards with animals and habitats and match them up, asking why they think that.
instructions: 1. Show a photo of an animal in its home (e.g., a camel in the desert). 2. Ask "Why does it have that?" (e.g., the long eyelashes or the hump). 3. Accept any logical answer—the goal is the *thinking process*, not the fact. 4. Look up the real reason together. 5. Have the child "invent" a new animal for a specific home (like the "Deep Dark Woods") and draw its special features.

title: colour match
description: see which colours you can see in the world around you.
instructions: 1. While on a walk or looking out the window, play "Color Match." 2. See how many different colors you can spot in the natural world. 3. Can you find something that is the *exact* same color as your shirt? 4. Discuss how colors change in different light (sun vs. shade). 5. This builds focused observation skills.

title: colour walk
info checked: go for a walk with your child and decide on a colour to follow, look around for it as you walk and walk towards the first thing of that colour that you see, if you can't see anything for a while go back the way that you came until you find something else of that colour. You can switch colours anytime you want, or you could do each colour of the rainbow once in ROYGBIV order or take turn deciding the next colour.

title: pom pom pop
description: put pom poms in sandwhich bag, with small hole, challange child to pop pom poms out
instructions: 1. Place pom-poms in a Ziploc bag and seal it. 2. Poke a hole in the corner of the bag just large enough for a pom-pom. 3. The child must use their fingers to "pop" or push the pom-poms out through the hole. 4. Count the pom-poms as they emerge. 5. This provides excellent resistance for building hand strength.

title: milk jug elephants
instructions: 1. Cut the handle and side of a milk jug to look like an elephant's trunk and head. 2. Paint the jug gray. 3. Add large paper ears to the sides. 4. Use the opening of the jug for the eyes or trunk detail. 5. Discuss how we can turn "rubbish" into a whole zoo of animals.

title: paper clip fishing
what you'll need: Paper fish with paperclips, magnet, string, stick
instructions: 1. Make a fishing rod using a stick and a magnet on a string. 2. Attach paperclips to paper fish. 3. Try to "catch" the fish from the floor. 4. Challenge: Try to catch the fish while standing on one leg! 5. Discuss how magnets pull on the metal paperclip.

title: measuring tape fishing
instructions: 1. Take a measuring tape around the house. 2. Find things that are exactly "10 centimeters" long. 3. Try to "fish" for long items by extending the tape. 4. Compare which is longer: the table or the sofa? 5. This introduces the concept of units and scale.

title: paper daffodils
instructions: 1. Cut yellow paper into petal shapes. 2. Glue them around the end of a green straw. 3. Add a small orange "cup" in the center made of paper. 4. Create a whole "bouquet" of paper daffodils. 5. Discuss how daffodils are one of the first signs of spring.

title: laminated flowers
instructions: 1. Collect flat flowers or petals. 2. Place them inside a laminating pouch or between contact paper. 3. Seal them to create "everlasting" flowers. 4. Hold them up to the light to see the details of the petals. 5. Use them as bookmarks or window decorations.

title: growing chia
what you'll need: Chia seeds, wet paper towel, tray
instructions: 1. Sprinkle chia seeds onto a damp paper towel in a tray. 2. Place in a sunny spot and keep the towel wet. 3. Watch as the seeds sprout "green hair" in just a few days. 4. Discuss what the seeds need to grow (water and light). 5. Measure how tall the "grass" grows each day.

title: Spring poems to learn about rhyming
description: make roses are red, violets are blue poems
instructions: 1. Read simple spring poems aloud. 2. Have the child "finish the rhyme" (e.g., "Roses are red, violets are..."). 3. Create your own simple 4-line poems about the weather or flowers. 4. Clapping to the rhythm of the poem helps with syllable awareness. 5. This builds the phonemic skills needed for early reading.

title: mirror me
description: just try mirroring your child and having them mirror you. You can see what each other can and can't copy.
instructions: 1. Sit opposite the child. 2. The child must "mirror" every move you make (slow arm movements, funny faces). 3. Switch roles and you mirror the child. 4. This builds focus and the ability to read non-verbal cues. 5. Discuss which movements were the hardest to copy.

title: Simon says
instructions: 1. Play "Simon Says." 2. If you say "Simon says touch your nose," the child does it. 3. If you just say "Touch your nose," they must stay still. 4. This develops "inhibitory control" (the ability to stop yourself from reacting). 5. Switch roles so the child can practice giving clear instructions.

title: bob the weasel
instructions: 1. One person hides an object while others have their eyes closed. 2. Give "hot" or "cold" clues as they search. 3. The person who finds it gets to hide it next. 4. This builds vocabulary for spatial awareness (e.g., "behind," "under"). 5. Discuss being a "fair" hider by picking good spots.
