title: grannys footsteps
instructions: 1. One child stands with their back to the group. 2. Another child "sneaks" up to touch their back. 3. The person in front must guess who touched them by their voice or footsteps. 4. This builds auditory focus and group bonding. 5. Discuss being very quiet while sneaking.

title: heads down, thumbs up
instructions: 1. "Granny" (the leader) stands at the end of the room with their back turned. 2. Children try to sneak up on Granny. 3. When Granny turns around, everyone must freeze. 4. If Granny sees you moving, you go back to the start. 5. This develops gross motor control and patience.

title: sweeping games
description: As boring as sweeping seems to us children don't do it much so when they get to sweep something up in school they love it. Here's some sweeping games you can do at home to make it a bit more interesting (and if you spread the items everywhere you want swept you'll have some very clean floors)
instructions: 1. Everyone sits with their heads down and eyes closed. 2. "Heads down, thumbs up!" 3. A few chosen children go around and gently touch one thumb each. 4. "Heads up, stand up!" 5. Those who were touched must guess who "tapped" them. 5. This builds social awareness and memory.
variations: everything could be done in teams with one child having the broom and the other a dustpan. put everything in the middle and see who can sweep up the most, spread them around the room and see who can sweep up the most, see how fast  everything can be swept up when everyone works together, use 2 differnt kinds or colours of items and they have to get only the ones they're supposed to, one child has a dustpan and brush and one has a broom and the one with the broom trys to stop the other from collecting all tge items

title: tree birds
description: to scale birds to hang from trees
instructions: 1. Spread small items (paper scraps, pom-poms) across the floor. 2. Have the child "sweep" the items into a specific taped-off square on the floor. 3. Once gathered, use the dustpan to collect them. 4. This develops the coordinated arm movements used for many chores. 5. Discuss how a clean floor makes a room safer and nicer to be in.

title: suet balls
instructions: 1. Look at photos of real birds. 2. Draw them "to scale" (the same size they are in real life). 3. Cut them out and hang them from tree branches outside. 4. Observe how they look against the real trees. 5. Discuss why birds might want to stay high up in the trees.

title: bubbles for cleaning
instructions: 1. Mix birdseed into softened lard or suet. 2. Press the mixture into the gaps of a pinecone or into a small ball. 3. Tie a string around it and hang it from a tree. 4. Observe from a window to see which birds come to eat. 5. Discuss how we can help animals find food during the winter or spring.

title: stone game
description: try and find stones that look like other things
what you'll need: Dish soap, water, cloth, dirty toys
instructions: 1. Set up a "wash station" with soapy water and a clean towel. 2. Provide a bin of "dirty" plastic toys (cars, animals). 3. Have the child scrub each toy with a cloth or brush until it is clean. 4. Rinse and dry the toys. 5. This builds a sense of responsibility and practices the "scrubbing" motion.

title: cloud watching
instructions: 1. Collect stones of many different shapes. 2. Turn them around and look at them from all sides. 3. Does this one look like a frog? Does that one look like a car? 4. Paint or draw on the stone to turn it into that object. 5. Discuss how our imagination helps us see new things in simple objects.

title: guess who variations
description: animals, story book characters, letters, numbers, dinosaurs
instructions: 1. Lie on your back on a clear day. 2. Look at the clouds as they move. 3. Ask "What does that cloud look like to you?" 4. Discuss how the wind changes the shapes of the clouds. 5. This is a great calm-down activity that develops creative thinking.

title: flying butterfly for cards
instructions: 1. Think of a category (e.g., Animals). 2. Give clues (e.g., "I am big, I am gray, I have a trunk"). 3. The child must "Guess Who" it is. 4. Switch roles—let the child pick a character and give you clues. 5. Use storybook characters or numbers for variety.

title: reverse colouring book
instructions: 1. Provide a "reverse coloring book" where the *colors* are already on the page but the *lines* are missing. 2. Have the child draw the outlines and details over the color splotches. 3. Discuss what they think each color should be (e.g., "This blue blob looks like a pond"). 4. This encourages creative interpretation of shapes. 5. Use black fineliners for the best effect.

title: elastic helicopter
instructions: 1. Build a small "helicopter" blade out of cardboard. 2. Use a rubber band and a stick to create a "launcher." 3. Hook the helicopter onto the rubber band, pull back, and release upwards. 4. Watch as the blades spin and lift the toy into the air. 5. Discuss how the spinning blades push the air down to lift the helicopter up.

title: shadow box
instructions: 1. Cut the bottom out of a box and cover it with tissue paper. 2. Place a flashlight inside the box. 3. Use your hands or cut-out silhouettes to make shadows on the tissue "screen." 4. Put on a shadow play for an audience. 5. Discuss how moving the light closer or further away changes the size of the shadow.

title: bouncing bubbles
description: bubbles that will bounce off fabric etc. but pop on bare skin, put your sleeve over your hand or wear gloves
what you'll need: Dish soap, glycerin (or corn syrup), fabric (sleeve/glove)
instructions: 1. Mix dish soap and water with a little glycerin to make "strong" bubbles. 2. Blow a bubble. 3. Try to "catch" and bounce the bubble on your sleeve or a wool glove. 4. Observe how the bubble pops instantly on skin but bounces off the fabric. 5. Discuss how the oil on our skin breaks the bubble's surface tension.

title: jumping spider
instructions: 1. Fold a small paper "spider." 2. Use a straw to blow air at the spider to make it "jump" or skitter. 3. Challenge: Can you make the spider jump over a pencil? 4. Try different sizes of paper to see which jumps furthest. 5. Discuss how the force of your breath moves the spider.

title: DIY chalk paint
instructions: 1. Crush chalk into a powder and mix with a little water and cornstarch. 2. Use paintbrushes to draw on the pavement or a chalkboard. 3. Observe how the paint "glows" when it is wet and turns into a dusty chalk when dry. 4. This is an easy way to make temporary outdoor art. 5. Discuss how the water evaporates to leave the chalk behind.

title: stereoscopy
description: download the 3d steriod app to take 3d images to explore with your child
instructions: 1. Download the Stereoid (or similar) 3D camera app. 2. Use it to take two slightly different photos of the same object. 3. View the images through a stereoscope or by "crossing your eyes" as directed by the app. 4. Observe how the flat images suddenly look 3D. 5. Discuss how our two eyes work together to see depth in the real world.

title: phonetic i spy
instructions: 1. Play "I Spy," but instead of saying the letter name, use the *phonetic sound* (e.g., "I spy with my little eye, something beginning with 'ssss'"). 2. The child must find objects that start with that sound (e.g., Sun, Socks). 3. This builds the foundational sound-recognition needed for spelling. 4. Discuss how different letters can make similar sounds. 5. Switch roles so the child can practice their sounds.

title: bubble snakes
instructions: 1. Dip a long string or tube into a bubble solution. 2. Blow slowly through one end to create a long "bubble snake." 3. See how long you can make the snake before it breaks. 4. Discuss how the soap stretches to hold the air inside. 5. This is a great outdoor sensory activity.

title: lateral thinking questions for kids
instructions: 1. Ask "Lateral Thinking" questions (e.g., "If you were as small as an ant, how would you get across this room?"). 2. There are no wrong answers—encourage the child to explain their reasoning. 3. Ask "What would happen if..." questions (e.g., "What if the sun never went down?"). 4. This develops the ability to think "outside the box" and solve problems creatively. 5. Discuss the different solutions you both come up with.
info checked:
1. The Red Knife
Question: Why are many special pocket knives (like Swiss Army knives) colored bright red?
Clue: Imagine you dropped one in the white snow.
Answer: So they are easy to find if you drop them! Red shows up very well against white snow.

2. The Quiet Lollipops
Question: Police officers once started giving free lollipops to noisy people leaving a party late at night. Why did they do that?
Clue: Try to shout while you are eating a sweet!
Answer: It is very hard to be noisy and shout when you are busy sucking on a lollipop. It kept them quiet!

3. Arrow Park
Question: A little girl asked her dad to take her to "Arrow Park." He took her to the swings, but she said "No." He took her to the slide, but she said "No." Finally, he realized she wanted to watch big machines landing from the sky. Where did she want to go?
Answer: The Airport! She thought the airplanes looked like big flying arrows.

4. The Clever Sheep
Question: Farmers put metal bars on the ground (called a cattle grid) to keep sheep inside a field. The sheep are usually too scared to walk on the bars because their feet might slip. But some clever sheep figured out a way to cross them without walking. How did they do it?
Answer: They rolled over them!

5. The Pizza Dots
Question: A pizza place (Domino’s) decided to put a dot on their logo for every new shop they opened. They had one dot, then two dots, then three... but soon they had to stop adding dots. Why?
Answer: They opened too many shops! They couldn't fit thousands of dots on the pizza box.

6. The Snowy Drive
Question: A man drives his small car to work in the morning. But when it is time to go home, he leaves his car at work and drives a giant truck home instead. Why?
Clue: He listened to the weather report and heard it was going to be a white night.
Answer: He drives a snowplow! He knew it was going to snow, so he took the plow home to clear the roads in the morning.

7. How Tall is a Smurf?
Question: You might know how tall you are in feet or centimetres. But in the cartoons, do you know how they measure a Smurf?
Clue: It involves a green fruit you might have in your lunchbox.
Answer: Apples! A Smurf is exactly "three apples high."
